en: Verses on the Distinction Between the Middle and the Extremes, One Fascicle.
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Only the obscuration of signs, the reality, and the cultivation of the various remedies—these stages of cultivation lead to the attainment of the fruit of the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
False conceptualization exists; within these two [the subject and object], both are entirely absent.
In this there is only emptiness, and in that there is also this.
Therefore it is said that all phenomena are neither empty nor non-empty;
because of existence, non-existence, and the presence of both, this accords with the Middle Way.
Consciousness arises and manifests as resembling objects, sentient beings, a self, and cognition;
these objects do not truly exist, and because the objects are absent, consciousness is absent.
The nature of false discrimination is established by this principle.
It is neither substantially existent nor entirely non-existent, for cessation and liberation are admitted [to exist].
It is explained as the imagined, the dependent, and the perfected natures,
because they are respectively the object, the conceptualization, and the emptiness of both.
Based on the apprehension of consciousness, the non-apprehension of objects arises;
based on the non-apprehension of objects, the non-apprehension of consciousness arises.
Because consciousness possesses the nature of apprehension, it likewise becomes non-apprehension.
Thus one knows that there are two kinds of attainment, yet the nature of non-attainment is equal.
The mind and mental factors of the three realms are false conceptualizations;
that which merely cognizes an object is called "mind," while those that function differently are separately termed "mental factors."
The first is called the consciousness that conditions; the second is named the experiencer, which herein performs the function of experiencing.
The mental factors (caitta) perform the functions of discernment and investigation.
Furthermore, there are those that obscure and conceal, those that establish, those that lead forward, those that gather, and those that bring to completion.
Because they consist of discrimination, enjoyment, instigation, binding,
manifestation, and the fruit of suffering, these alone afflict the world:
the three, two, and seven types of defilement arise from false conceptualization.
The various characteristics, the alternative designations, the distinctions of meaning, and their establishment—
know that the two kinds of emptiness are briefly explained solely by these.
Because there is neither duality nor existence and non-existence, it is neither existent nor non-existent.
Neither different nor identical—this is explained as the characteristic of emptiness.

To briefly state the various synonyms for emptiness: one should know them to be suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), signlessness (*animitta*), the ultimate nature (*paramārthatā*), the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*), and so forth.
Because it is unchanging and non-erroneous, because it is the sphere of noble wisdom where signs have ceased,
and because it is the cause of all noble dharmas— these are the meanings of the various synonyms,
respectively. This [reality] is both defiled and purified, by virtue of being with stains and without stains.
Just as the elements of water, gold, and space are considered pure because they are pure, so too are the eater and the eaten; these depend upon the body in which they abide.
One who can perceive this principle will attain the two purities sought through emptiness.
To constantly benefit sentient beings, to not abandon saṃsāra,
and for goodness to be inexhaustible, one contemplates this as empty.
To purify the spiritual lineage (gotra) and to attain the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana), one contemplates this as empty.
To purify all Buddha-dharmas, the Bodhisattva contemplates emptiness.
Since both the person (pudgala) and dharmas lack any real intrinsic nature,
these two— non-existence and existence— are established separately as the two kinds of emptiness.
If this were not subject to defilement, all would be liberated by themselves;
if this were not subject to purification, effort would be fruitless.
It is neither defiled nor non-defiled; it is neither pure nor non-pure.
Because the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure, it is defiled by adventitious stains.
Whether in their entirety or in part, whether predominant or equal,
regarding the grasping and abandoning within saṃsāra, two kinds of obstacles to the two natures are taught.
The nine types of afflictive characteristics refer to the nine fetters, such as craving and so forth;
the first two obstruct disenchantment and equanimity, while the remaining seven obstruct true vision.
That is to say, they can obstruct [the vision of] the view of a self, its object, cessation, the path, and the Jewels.
Because they have distanced themselves from the thorough knowledge of gain, honor, and the like;
because there is no application of effort and no improper objects;
because they do not arise through correct reasoning and fail to give rise to right reflection; and because their provisions are not yet perfected.
Lacking the spiritual lineage and virtuous friends, with a mind characterized by extreme weariness and exhaustion, and lacking in correct practice; dwelling together with those who are base and evil;
the three remaining [obstructions] of invertedness and coarse heaviness; and the non-attainment of *prajñā*.
As well as the natural heaviness of the fundamental nature, the nature of indolence and negligence;
attachment to existence and to material wealth, as well as a base and inferior mental disposition;
lack of faith and absence of resolute conviction; and grasping at the meaning according to the literal expression.
Disregarding the Dharma while valuing fame and profit, lacking compassion for sentient beings,
being destitute of learning or possessing but little learning, and failing to cultivate sublime meditative concentration— these are the obstacles.
Being embraced by the excellence of bodhicitta, possessing wisdom, and being free from the obstacle of distraction [are the qualities].
Dedicating [merit] without fear of stinginess, Mastery, and so forth, are called "the virtuous" and the like.
These ten, such as the virtuous and so forth, Each have the three aforementioned obstacles.
One should know that regarding the factors of enlightenment, the perfections, and the stages, There are distinct obstacles.
Lacking skill regarding objects, possessing both laziness and diminished concentration,
lacking the capacity for growth and being of a weak nature, and seeing only the faults of grossness—
these are the obscurations to wealth and status, to the happy realms, and to not abandoning sentient beings.
Regarding the decrease and increase of faults and virtues, causing [beings] to enter and attain liberation;
hindering generosity and other virtues; being inexhaustible and uninterrupted;
the certainty of what is done for the sake of virtue; and the maturation of the enjoyment of the Dharma.
Pervasive and supreme, The flow of excellence and non-appropriation,
Continuity without distinction, Neither defiled nor purified,
The non-differentiation of various phenomena, And neither increasing nor decreasing.
Together with non-discrimination and so forth, these are the meanings of the four masteries.
Within these ten dharma-realms, there exists undefiled ignorance which obstructs the merits of the ten stages; therefore, they are called the ten obstacles.
The various afflictions and the cognitive obscurations have already been explained;
by the admission that these two are exhausted, one is liberated from all obscurations.
The realities are truly tenfold, namely: the fundamental [nature] and its characteristics.
Non-inversion, cause and effect, Coarseness and subtlety, reality, consensus,
The sphere of the pure, inclusion, and differentiation—
These ten types of skillful reality Are all for the purpose of eliminating the view of self.
It is admitted that among the three natures, one is eternally non-existent;
one exists but is not real; and one exists as reality.
This applies to phenomena, the person, and the grasped and the grasper.
Within the nature of existence and non-existence, there are views of superimposition and denial;
by knowing this, one does not waver—this is called the characteristic of reality.
The absence of nature, arising and ceasing, and the three types of impermanence regarding defilement and purity;
The grasped object, the objective entity, and their characteristics—these three aspects of suffering are combined;
emptiness likewise has three kinds, namely: non-existence, difference, and intrinsic nature;
signlessness, difference from signs, and self-characteristic—these are the three types of selflessness.
Respectively, these four and three types are based on the fundamental reality (*mūlatattva*).
Having already explained the three characteristics of suffering (*duḥkha*), there are likewise three types of origination (*samudaya*):
namely, habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), co-arising (*samutthāna*), and the characteristic of non-separation from bondage (*aviyogalakṣaṇa*).
Intrinsic nature, the two types of non-arising, The two cessations of defilement and tranquility,
Thorough knowledge and permanent abandonment, And the realization of the truths of the three paths—
One should know that conventional truth Is distinguished by these three kinds.
That is to say: the provisional, the conditioned, and the manifest, which correspond respectively to the first three [bases].
The ultimate truth is also threefold: namely, the object, attainment, and correct practice;
these rely on the single [base], are unchanging, non-erroneous, and perfectly real.
Worldly consensus relies on one; logical consensus relies on three.
The pure object of engagement has two [aspects], relying on one: the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
That which is named the "imagined" (*parikalpita*) is the characteristic; the "dependent" (*paratantra*) is conceptual differentiation.
Suchness and correct cognition are subsumed within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The process of evolution (*pravṛtti*) and the established order (*vyavasthāna*) depend on the first two [natures].
The true characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), and purity depend solely on the latter one. Correct practice (*samyak-pratipatti*) depends on the final one.
Regarding the view of a self (*ātman*) in the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth: it is grasped as being one, a cause, an experiencer, an agent,
one who acts with sovereignty, a dominant factor, permanent,
the basis of defilement and purification, and the nature of that which contemplates, binds, and liberates.
This grasped object and the discrimination [of it]—the meaning of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) resides therein.
That which is not one, nor a whole, but is divided into parts, is called a "skandha" (aggregate).
The grasper, the grasped, and that which grasps—the meaning of their seeds—is called a "dhātu" (element).
The sense-faculties as the receivers and the objects as that which are cognized—these, in terms of their functional gateways, are called "bases" (āyatana).
Regarding the meaning of dependent origination, there is neither increase nor decrease in cause, fruit, or function.
Regarding the disagreeable, the agreeable, the pure, Co-arising, and the sovereign, As well as attainment,
and lack of mastery over formations— This is the meaning of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna*).
Based on grasping, abiding, continuity, function, and the predominance of the two purities;
the meaning of "world" (*loka*) should be understood as the cause and effect of what has been used and what has not yet been used.
Feeling and the requisites for feeling, the formative forces that cause them,
the two kinds of cessation, and their antidotes— these are to be known as the meaning of the truths.
Furthermore, by way of virtues and faults, and through non-conceptual wisdom, [the truths are to be understood].
One should understand the meaning of this vehicle as that which leads to liberation from the dependent nature.
The meanings of the conditioned and the unconditioned refer to: the conventional, the causal, and the characteristic;
as well as tranquility and the object of its observation.
Because the cause of craving for the coarse and heavy (dauṣṭhulya) is the non-delusion regarding the self-entity,
one should know that the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are cultivated in order to enter the Four Noble Truths.
Having thoroughly understood the obstacles and their remedies in all their various aspects, [one proceeds].
To cultivate detachment through practice, diligently apply the four right efforts.
Abiding in the state of fitness for action to accomplish all tasks,
eliminate the five faults by diligently practicing the eight applications of abandonment.
Laziness, forgetting the sacred words, as well as lethargy,
agitation, non-application, and over-application— these five faults should be known.
To eliminate indolence, one cultivates desire, diligence, faith, and serenity;
these constitute the basis and that which is based upon it, as well as the cause and its result.
To eliminate the remaining four faults, one cultivates mindfulness, wisdom, reflection, and equanimity;
by noting sinking and agitation, one suppresses their activity and brings about their cessation and subsequent flow.
Having already planted the seeds conducive to liberation, one further cultivates the five superior qualities:
namely, aspiration, application, non-forgetfulness, non-distraction, and discernment.
The power [of the faculties] is defined by the impairment of obstacles; their sequence is established according to cause and effect.
Two pairs of factors conducive to penetration reside within the five faculties and the five powers.
Briefly stated, there are five branches of enlightenment, namely: the basis, the intrinsic nature, and so forth.
Renunciation and benefit, as well as the three factors free from defilement—
due to their causal conditions, their basis, and the distinctions in their intrinsic natures,
pliancy, concentration, and equanimity are taught as the factors free from defilement.
Through discernment and instruction, one causes others to believe in the three [jewels];
likewise, there are three remedies for the obstacles. Thus, the branches of the path are established as eight.
By manifesting right view and the restraint of morality, one causes others to have deep faith and acceptance.
Because they counteract the root and secondary afflictions, as well as the obstacles to mastery;
because they are inverted yet conform to the non-inverted, follow the non-inverted while being inverted,
or follow the non-inverted while being non-inverted— these are the distinctions in their cultivation and purification.
Because the bodhisattvas’ cultivation, through the mental engagement with the object of focus,
results in the realization of excellence, it differs from that of the two vehicles.
Regarding the cultivation of remedies that has been explained, there are eighteen stages.
That is to say: cause, entrance, practice, fruit; action, non-action, excellence, superior, unsurpassed;
the stage of conduct through aspiration, entry, renunciation, prediction, explanation, consecration, and realization;
benefit, and the accomplishment of what is to be done.
One should know that within the *dharmadhātu*, there are briefly three stages:
the impure, the impure-pure, and the pure, as appropriate.
Based on these aforementioned stages, all their various differentiated characteristics [are to be understood].
The various types of *pudgalas* are established according to what is appropriate.
The "vessel" is said to be the maturation (*vipāka*); power is its dominant influence (*adhipati*);
and the increase of delight and purity are, respectively, the five fruits.

Furthermore, the remaining fruits are briefly explained: the subsequent, the initial, the repeated practice, the ultimate, the conforming, the cessation of obstacles, the detachment, the superior, and the unsurpassed.
Because it is based entirely upon these three unsurpassed aspects, it is called the Unsurpassed Vehicle (Anuttarayāna).
That is to say: right practice, the object of focus, and the cultivation and realization of the unsurpassed.
Right practice has six types: namely, the most excellent, attention, conformity to the Dharma, avoidance of the two extremes, differentiation, and non-differentiation.
The supreme [perfections] are twelvefold: namely, vastness, long duration, basis, and inexhaustibility;
continuity, lack of difficulty, mastery, inclusion, initiation, attainment, outflow, and culmination.
Based on this, the ten perfections are taught; they are called *pāramitās*.
The ten *pāramitās* are: generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, aspiration, power, and knowledge.
Benefiting others, non-harming, receiving, increasing virtue, being able to enter, liberation, inexhaustibility,
constant arising, meditative concentration, and the enjoyment of maturing others.
The Bodhisattva, by means of the three types of wisdom, constantly contemplates the Mahāyāna;
according to the dharmas as they have been established, this is called "mental attention" (*manasikāra*) and "correct practice.
This increases the realm of the wholesome, leading to the penetration of meaning and the accomplishment of tasks.
These accompanying factors should be known as the ten types of Dharma practice:
namely, writing, making offerings, giving to others, listening, reading aloud,
receiving and upholding, correctly expounding, reciting, reflecting, and cultivating.
One who practices the ten dharmas attains an immeasurable mass of merit;
because it is supreme and inexhaustible, it arises from ceaselessly gathering others.
There are two kinds of practice in accordance with the Dharma, namely, those that are free from distraction.
The absence of inversion and transformation— these are what the bodhisattvas should know.
Emerging from meditative absorption, flowing toward objects, attachment and laxity or agitation,
feigning, self-grasping, and mental inferiority— these are what the wise should know.
Wisdom perceives the meaning of the text; it involves mental attention and is immovable.
It possesses two aspects—defilement and purity—which are adventitious. It is free from fear and pride, and is non-erroneous.
One should know that this occurs solely through association, through habitual practice, or by the reverse of these.
That there is existence and non-existence is non-erroneous regarding the words.
That they appear as having a dual nature, yet do not exist in reality,
and knowing them to be free from both existence and non-existence, is non-erroneous regarding the meaning.

Regarding non-erroneous attention (*manasikāra*): one knows that verbal expression is an imprint (*vāsanā*), and that verbal expression is its basis, because it appears as the cause for both [the object and the cognition].
Regarding non-erroneous immovability (*aniñjya*): this refers to knowing that the object does not exist.
It is not that things such as illusions do not exist, for existence and non-existence are immovable.
Regarding their own characteristics without error, one knows that all are merely names;
free from all conceptual construction, one relies upon the ultimate own-characteristic.
Since there is not a single phenomenon that exists apart from the true dharma-realm,
one who thoroughly penetrates this is unerring regarding common characteristics.
One knows whether the attention of inversion has been extinguished or has not yet been extinguished.
Regarding the defilement and purification of the dharmadhātu, there is no inversion.
Knowing that the intrinsic nature of the dharmadhātu is as pure as space, one understands that defilement and purification have no master;
this is non-inversion regarding adventitious [phenomena].
Because sentient beings and phenomena do not exist, both the nature of defilement and purity are absent;
knowing this, one is free from fear and pride—this is non-erroneousness regarding these two.
As for difference and identity, the outsiders and the śrāvakas [hold opposing views].
The extremes of superimposition and denial each apply to both sentient beings and phenomena;
likewise for the objects to be remedied and their remedies, eternalism and nihilism,
the extremes of grasped object and grasping subject, and the two types of defilement and purification.
The nature of the two extremes should be understood as being further sevenfold:
namely, the extremes of existence and non-existence; the tranquil and the fearful;
the grasped and the grasper; the correct and the false; and that which is functional and that which is non-functional.
Non-arising, arising, and so forth— these are the conceptualizations of the two extremes.
One should know that regarding the ten stages and the ten perfections, there is the cultivation and accumulation of their distinctions and non-distinctions through the modes of increase and so on.
The objects of focus (ālambana) are: placement, realm, that which is established, sustenance, internal sealing, penetration, increase, realization, transport, and supremacy.

Cultivation and realization consist of: being without deficiency, being indestructible and immovable, being complete, arising, being firm, being pliant, not abiding, and the cessation of obstructions.
This treatise elucidates the Middle and the Extremes, The profound, secret, firm, and substantial meaning, And the vastness of all meanings;
It dispels all inauspiciousness. *Madhyāntavibhāga-kārikā* (Verses on the Discrimination of the Middle and the Extremes)
